title: Direct & Indirect Speech
summary: Two narration items per shift, all built from four moving parts: reporting verb, backshift ladder, pronoun anchors and the time/place word table. Statement, question, command, request and exclamation each have one fixed skeleton — learn the skeletons plus the exceptions (universal truths, frozen modals) and narration becomes a formula topic, both directions.

subtopics.title: Reporting verbs and the mechanics of the shift
subtopics.concept:
Direct speech quotes the speaker's words inside inverted commas; indirect (reported) speech folds them into the reporter's sentence. Three mechanical changes always apply:

1. **Comma and quotes vanish; a connective appears.** Statements take **that**: He said, "I am tired" → He said **that** he was tired.
2. **The reporting verb fits the mood.** *said to* → **told** (+ listener) or said (+ that); a question → **asked** (never 'asked that' for yes/no — use if/whether); a command → **ordered/told/commanded**; advice → **advised**; request → **requested**; suggestion → **suggested/proposed**; warning → **warned**.
3. **Word order in questions becomes statement order** — auxiliary before subject dies: He said to her, "Where **do you live**?" → He asked her where **she lived**.

**Tone-fitting table:**

| Direct situation | Reporting verb | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Plain statement | said / told me | said that … / told me that … |
| Command | ordered, told, commanded | told/ordered + object + to + V1 |
| Advice | advised | advised + object + to + V1 |
| Request (please, kindly) | requested | requested + object + to + V1 |
| Negative command | forbade / told … not to | told + object + not to + V1 |
| Suggestion (Let us…) | suggested, proposed | suggested + V-ing / that … should |
| Exclamation (Hurrah!, Alas!) | exclaimed with joy/sorrow | exclaimed … that + statement |
| Wish (Good morning!) | wished | wished + object |
| Thanks | thanked | thanked + object (+ for …) |

**'Said me' does not exist** — said needs 'to' (said to me) or becomes told (told me). This one letter difference is the most planted distractor in the section.

tricks.title: Verb-tone match
tricks.body: Read the quoted words first for TONE: order, advice, request, question, joy, sorrow. Then pick the reporting verb that carries that tone — the verb choice alone often eliminates two options.

tricks.title: said-to vs told
tricks.body: said + to + person; told + person. Any 'said me' or 'told to me' option is dead on arrival.

tricks.title: Connective test
tricks.body: Statement → that. Yes/no question → if/whether (never that). Wh-question → the wh-word itself (never if).

mistakes: Writing 'He said me' — said never takes a direct listener.
Using 'asked that' for a yes/no question instead of 'asked if'.
Keeping inverted commas or a comma after the reporting verb.
Choosing 'ordered' where the sentence asks politely — tone mismatch.
subtopics.notes:
### The reporting verb is the first word you write
Direct: *She said to me, 'I am tired.'* Indirect: *She told me that she was tired.* The comma and the inverted commas die; a connector takes their place; and the reporting verb itself often changes. Get the verb right and half the item is already done.

### say vs tell
- **tell needs a listener**: told me, told us, told him. Exam English never accepts *told that...* with no object after told.
- **say needs no listener**: *He said that...*
- **said to + listener becomes told + listener**: *He said to me* → *He told me*.
The giveaway: if the stem reads *said to someone*, the keyed option begins with told/asked/ordered-type verb plus that someone — never 'said to' kept as it is.

### The tone of the quote picks the verb
| Quote tone | Reporting verb | Connector |
|---|---|---|
| Statement | told / said | that |
| Yes/No question | asked | if / whether |
| Wh-question | asked | the wh-word itself |
| Order | ordered / told + object | to + V1 |
| Request (please, kindly) | requested | to + V1 |
| Advice | advised | to + V1 |
| Suggestion (let us) | suggested / proposed | V-ing, or that...should |
| Exclamation of joy (Hurrah) | exclaimed with joy | that |
| Exclamation of grief (Alas) | exclaimed with sorrow | that |
| Wish / prayer | wished / prayed | that |

Match tone to verb: a please-sentence keyed with *ordered* is wrong even when every tense inside is perfect. Exams plant exactly this — the correct tenses wrapped around the wrong verb.

### Present or future reporting verb: no backshift
If the reporting verb is present (says, asks, has said) or future (will say), the quote's tense does NOT move: *He says, 'I am busy.'* → *He says that he **is** busy.* An option offering *was* or *would* there is the planted fault. Papers also like the reporting verb swapped quietly: *says* keyed as *said*.

### Connector discipline
- Statements → **that**.
- Yes/No questions → **if** or **whether** (never both, never that).
- Orders, requests, advice → **to + base verb** (never that, never that...to).
Exactly one connector per sentence: *asked that if* and *told that to come* are impossible — each is a favourite wrong option.

### Other mechanics
- The inverted commas, the comma after the reporting verb, the capital letter of the quote and the question mark all disappear; the reported sentence ends with a full stop.
- The listener stays in the object case: told **me**, asked **him**, requested **her**.
- A listener after told is compulsory: *told the staff*, never *told to the staff*.
- With say + universal sentence, that is still the connector: *He said that honesty is the best policy.*

### Quick revision
- said to + person → told + person; tell always takes a listener, say never does.
- Tone map: statement → that; yes/no → if/whether; wh → the wh-word; order/request/advice → to + V1; Hurrah → exclaimed with joy; Alas → exclaimed with sorrow.
- Reporting verb in the present (says/asks/has said) → NO backshift inside.
- One connector only; that never pairs with if/whether/to.
- told takes its object directly: told the staff, not told to the staff.

patterns.name: said to + listener becomes told + listener
patterns.howToSpot: The stem reads 'X said to me/him/us, ...' with a statement; one option keeps 'said to', one drops the listener after told, and the keyed one reads told + listener + that.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot said to + a person: that pair must become told + the person.
2. Add the connector that and run the rest of the checks (tense ladder, pronouns, time words).
3. Kill options that keep said to, or that use told with no listener, or told to + listener.

*Why it works:* say never carries a listener while tell must — the exam plants one option that forgets each half.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *She said to me, 'I am very busy today.'*
example.solution: **She told me that she was very busy that day.** — said to me → told me; am → was; today → that day. Keeping 'said to me that...' is the planted fault.

patterns.name: Tone decides the reporting verb
patterns.howToSpot: The stem carries please/kindly (request), an order, advice, or a suggestion; the options use different verbs (requested/ordered/advised/suggested) with identical tenses.
patterns.logic:
1. Classify the tone before touching anything else: please → requested; command → ordered; advice → advised; let us → suggested.
2. Attach the right frame: requested/ordered/advised + object + to + V1; suggested + V-ing.
3. Reject options whose tense work is fine but whose verb mismatches the tone.

*Why it works:* tone-to-verb is a one-to-one map, so the verb alone can settle the item even before the tenses are compared.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The doctor said to Father, 'Give up smoking.'*
example.solution: Advice tone → **The doctor advised Father to give up smoking.** 'Requested Father' softens a piece of advice into a favour; 'ordered Father' hardens it — both are planted.

patterns.name: Present reporting verb: no backshift
patterns.howToSpot: The stem's frame is says / often says / has said / will say; one option backshifts the quote (is → was, will → would) and the keyed one leaves the tense untouched.
patterns.logic:
1. Check the reporting verb's tense FIRST.
2. Present or future frame → the quote's tense and time words stay exactly as spoken (only pronouns follow SONA).
3. Also reject options that quietly swap says → said.

*Why it works:* backshift exists to mark remoteness in time; a present reporting verb has none, so the ladder is not climbed.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *Ravi says, 'I do not like loud music.'*
example.solution: **Ravi says that he does not like loud music.** — says keeps the quote in the present: does not like, NOT did not like. Only the pronoun moves (I → he).

patterns.name: Connector discipline (one connector, right one)
patterns.howToSpot: Options that pair connectors (asked that if, told that to) or keep the do/does/did of the quote inside a reported question.
patterns.logic:
1. Statement → that; yes/no question → if/whether; wh-question → the wh-word alone; order/request/advice → to + V1.
2. Count the connectors in each option — exactly one is allowed.
3. In reported questions, do/does/did of the direct quote must vanish, with the tense landing on the main verb.

*Why it works:* English allows one subordinator per clause; stacking two (or keeping an auxiliary with nothing to carry) is always wrong.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *Priya asked me, 'Are you coming to the fair?'*
example.solution: **Priya asked me if I was coming to the fair.** — one connector (if), statement order after it. 'Asked me that if...' stacks two connectors; 'if was I coming' breaks the order.

subtopics.title: Backshift: the tense conversion table
subtopics.concept:
When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, asked — nearly always in SSC), every tense inside the quotes moves one step back:

| Direct (quoted) tense | Indirect tense | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Simple present (V1) | Simple past (V2) | "I **write**" → he **wrote** |
| Present continuous | Past continuous | "I **am writing**" → he **was writing** |
| Present perfect | Past perfect | "I **have written**" → he **had written** |
| Present perfect continuous | Past perfect continuous | "I **have been writing**" → he **had been writing** |
| Simple past (V2) | Past perfect | "I **wrote**" → he **had written** |
| Past continuous | Past perfect continuous (or past perfect) | "I **was writing**" → he **had been writing** |
| will | would | "I **will** come" → he **would** come |
| can | could | "I **can** help" → he **could** help |
| may | might | "I **may** come" → he **might** come |
| shall | should (with I/we) | "I **shall** go" → I **should** go |
| must | must / had to | "I **must** go" → he **must/had to** go |
| have to | had to | "I **have to** go" → he **had to** go |

**Verbs that NEVER backshift:** past perfect (had written stays had written), could, would, should, might, ought to, used to, should have. If the quote already uses one of these, the tense is settled — options changing it are wrong.

**The universal-truth exception:** scientific facts, habitual truths and proverbs **keep their tense** even after a past reporting verb: The teacher said that **the earth revolves** around the sun (not 'revolved'). Habitual actions with always/every day may also stay in the present. This exception appears in nearly every shift — one item, whole mark.

tricks.title: One-step-back ladder
tricks.body: Recite the ladder: present→past, present cont.→past cont., perfect→past perfect, past→past perfect, will→would, can→could, may→might, must→had to.

tricks.title: Frozen-five
tricks.body: could, would, should, might, ought to never change. Spot one in the quote → that option's tense is already correct; any shift is an error.

tricks.title: Truth test
tricks.body: Is the quoted statement a fact of nature, a habit or a proverb? Then no backshift — said that the earth REVOLVES.

mistakes: Backshifting past perfect to something nonexistent (had had written).
Forgetting the universal-truth exception and 'revolved' the sun.
Backshifting 'must' to 'musted' — it becomes must or had to.
Changing 'could' to 'can' in indirect speech — the frozen modals never move.
subtopics.notes:
### The ladder: one rung down
When the reporting verb is in the past — said, told, asked, nearly always in exams — every verb inside the quote steps ONE rung down:

| Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|
| am / is / are | was / were |
| write (V1) | wrote (V2) |
| is / are writing | was / were writing |
| has / have written | had written |
| wrote (V2) | had written |
| was / were writing | had been writing |
| will / shall | would / should |
| can | could |
| may | might |
| must (duty) | had to |

'I am writing a letter' → he said he **was writing** a letter. 'I wrote it' → he said he **had written** it.

### The ceiling: past perfect never climbs
A quote already in the past perfect stays where it is: 'The train had left' → he said the train **had left**. Same for the past perfect continuous. There is no fifth rung.

### Where the ladder is not used
- **Universal truths and habits of nature**: 'The earth revolves around the sun' → he said that the earth **revolves** around the sun.
- **Present or future reporting verb**: says/asks/will say → no change at all.
- **Unreal and fixed forms**: would, could, might, should, ought to, used to, had better, would rather — these are already one step from reality and do NOT shift again. 'I would rather stay home' → he said he **would rather stay** home.

### The two planted traps
- **Over-backshift**: 'I am tired' reported as *he said he had been tired* — one rung too far. Simple present steps to simple past, never straight to the past perfect.
- **Half-backshift**: the frame is said but the quote still carries is, are, will, can. This is the single commonest wrong option in the section.

### Time words travel with the tense
The backshift drags the time words along: tomorrow → the next day, now → then, ago → before. If an option backshifts the verb but keeps tomorrow — or shifts the time word but keeps is — kill it. Tense and time words move together or not at all; that pairing is itself a testable pattern.

### Modal specifics worth memorising
must for obligation → had to ('I must reach by six' → he said he **had to** reach by six); must for deduction can stay must. would rather, had better and used to are frozen — they never change shape, only the pronouns around them move.

### Quick revision
- One rung: am → was; write → wrote; was writing → had been writing; wrote → had written; will → would; can → could; may → might; must (duty) → had to.
- had + V3 is the ceiling: it stays had + V3.
- No shift for universal truths, present reporting verbs, and would/could/might/should/ought to/used to/had better/would rather.
- Over-backshift and half-backshift are the two planted faults — count the rungs.
- Verb moved? Time words must move too.

patterns.name: Present to past: the first rung
patterns.howToSpot: The quote is in the simple present or present continuous; the options differ between was/were (correct rung) and had been (over-shift) or is/are (no shift).
patterns.logic:
1. Confirm the reporting verb is past (said/told/asked).
2. Step the quote down exactly one rung: am/is + V-ing → was/were + V-ing; V1 → V2.
3. Refuse both neighbours: the unshifted present and the over-shifted past perfect continuous.

*Why it works:* the first rung is the most-set row in the paper, and its two wrong neighbours are always planted.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *He said, 'I am learning German these days.'*
example.solution: **He said that he was learning German those days.** — am learning steps to was learning; these days → those days. 'Had been learning' climbs two rungs.

patterns.name: Past to past perfect: the second rung
patterns.howToSpot: The quote uses a simple past or past continuous verb; options offer the unshifted past, the correct had-forms, or a present perfect.
patterns.logic:
1. V2 inside a past frame → had + V3.
2. was/were + V-ing → had been + V-ing (past continuous → past perfect continuous).
3. Remember the ceiling: a quote already in the past perfect does not move.

*Why it works:* the earlier-of-two-past-events rule carries over into reporting — the reported event must read as before the reporting.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The watchman said, 'The lights were flickering all night.'*
example.solution: **The watchman said that the lights had been flickering all night.** — were flickering steps to had been flickering. 'Had flickered' changes the continuous to a completed act.

patterns.name: Modal shifts (will, can, may, must)
patterns.howToSpot: The quote carries will/can/may/must; options swap in the unshifted modal, a neighbouring wrong modal, or the correct would/could/might/had to.
patterns.logic:
1. Apply the modal row: will/shall → would/should; can → could; may → might; must (duty) → had to.
2. Keep the rest of the verb phrase untouched (will visit → would visit, not had visited).
3. Pair the modal check with the time word check in the same sweep.

*Why it works:* each modal has exactly one partner one rung down; anything else (may → will, will → had) is a planted neighbour.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *She said, 'I can solve this puzzle.'*
example.solution: **She said that she could solve that puzzle.** — can → could. 'Can solve' refuses the shift; 'may solve' imports the wrong modal.

patterns.name: No backshift: universal truth
patterns.howToSpot: The quote states a law of nature, a proverb, or a permanent fact ('The sun rises in the east'); one option dutifully backshifts it (rose) and the keyed one keeps the present.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask: is the statement true always, or only at the moment of speaking?
2. Always-true → the tense stays put even inside a past frame.
3. Moment-bound facts (I am tired) shift normally.

*Why it works:* the backshift marks remoteness; a truth that has not stopped being true is not remote, so exams keep it in the present.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The teacher said, 'The sun rises in the east.'*
example.solution: **The teacher said that the sun rises in the east.** — a law of nature keeps its present tense. 'Rose in the east' is the classic planted backshift.

patterns.name: Frozen forms: would rather, used to
patterns.howToSpot: The quote already contains would/could/used to/had better/would rather; the wrong options re-shift them (had used to, had rather) or break their shape.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the unreal/fixed form in the quote.
2. Copy it unchanged — only the pronoun and time words around it move.
3. Reject options that add had to them or convert their verb (used to swam).

*Why it works:* these forms are already one step away from the real present; the ladder has no rung below them, so they freeze.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *She said, 'I used to swim every morning.'*
example.solution: **She said that she used to swim every morning.** — used to stays used to; only I → she moves. 'Had used to swim' invents an impossible extra rung.

subtopics.title: Pronouns, and the time/place word table
subtopics.concept:
**Pronouns change by who is speaking to whom** (the SONA logic): **first person follows the reporter**, **second person follows the listener**, **third person never changes**.

He said to me, "**I** will help **you** with **your** work" → He told me that **he** would help **me** with **my** work. (I → he: speaker; you → me: listener; your → my.)

He said to Ram, "**You** must bring **your** book" → He told Ram that **he** had to bring **his** book. (you → he: the listener Ram; your → his.)

**The time/place table** — every word anchored to the speaker's 'now and here' shifts to the reporter's distance:

| Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|
| now | then |
| today | that day |
| tonight | that night |
| yesterday | the previous day / the day before |
| tomorrow | the next day / the following day |
| the day after tomorrow | two days later |
| last week/month | the previous week/month |
| next week/month | the following week/month |
| ago | before / earlier |
| hence | thence |
| here | there |
| this | that |
| these | those |
| thus | so |
| come | go (when perspective shifts) |

**When the reporting verb is in the PRESENT** (says, is saying — rare in SSC but tested in Tier 2), neither tense nor time words change: He says, "I **am** busy **today**" → He says that he **is** busy **today**.

tricks.title: SONA sweep
tricks.body: Mark the three pronoun anchors before touching anything else: 1st person → speaker, 2nd person → listener, 3rd person → unchanged. Most wrong options botch exactly one of these.

tricks.title: Yesterday/tomorrow pair
tricks.body: yesterday → the previous day; tomorrow → the next (following) day. The pair travels together — if one shifted and the option leaves the other, it's wrong.

tricks.title: Present-reporter exemption
tricks.body: Reporting verb 'says' (present) → nothing shifts: tense AND time words freeze. Check the reporting verb before applying any table.

mistakes: Leaving 'you' unchanged when the listener is named (Ram → he).
Writing 'yesterday' or 'tomorrow' inside reported speech.
Changing 'this' to 'the' instead of 'that'.
Shifting tenses because the sentence 'looks indirect' even when the reporter says (present).
subtopics.notes:
### Pronouns: the SONA rule
- **First person (I, we, my, our) follows the reporter** — the subject outside the quotes.
- **Second person (you, your) follows the listener** — the person addressed, usually the object of the reporting verb.
- **Third person (he, she, it, they) never changes.**

*He said to me, 'I will explain the sum to you.'* → He told me that **he** would explain the sum to **me**. The I belongs to the speaker (he), the you to the listener (me). Say the two anchors aloud — reporter and listener — and the mapping writes itself.

Worked grid: *Sita said to Gita, 'You are late.'* → Sita told Gita that **she** was late (you = the listener Gita). *The guests said, 'We enjoyed it.'* → The guests said that **they** had enjoyed it (we = the speakers themselves). Track the speaker's gender too: a female speaker's I becomes **she**, not he.

### The time table — learn it as one block
| Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|
| now | then |
| today | that day |
| tonight | that night |
| tomorrow | the next day / the following day |
| yesterday | the previous day / the day before |
| last night / last week | the previous night / the previous week |
| ago | before |
| hence | thence |
| next Monday / next month | the following Monday / the following month |
| thus | so |

### The place and demonstrative table
| Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|
| this | that |
| these | those |
| here | there |
| come | go |
| bring | take |

*Meet me here tomorrow morning* → he asked me to meet him **there** **the next** morning. Note come → go shifts only when the speaker's viewpoint moves: reporting 'I will come' from elsewhere turns come into go.

### The pairing rule (the real test)
Tense and time words move TOGETHER. An option that writes *would visit ... tomorrow* — modal shifted, time word left — is wrong, and so is *will visit ... the next day*. In a well-set item, one wrong option shifts the verb only, one shifts the time word only, and one shifts both. The one that shifts both is the answer.

### Three pronoun traps planted in options
- Keeping **you/your** inside a told-me sentence — the listener was ignored.
- **Random promotion**: I turned into the wrong person (he instead of she, or her instead of me).
- **Number slips**: we → he instead of they.

### Quick revision
- SONA: 1st person → reporter's subject; 2nd person → the listener; 3rd person untouched.
- tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day; ago → before; now → then; today → that day; next → the following; last → the previous.
- this → that; these → those; here → there; come → go; bring → take.
- Tense shifted but time word kept (or the reverse) = planted fault; both move together.
- Check the speaker's gender before writing his/her.

patterns.name: SONA pronoun mapping
patterns.howToSpot: The quote has I/we/you/my/your and the options differ only in the pronouns (to me / to you / to him; she was / you were).
patterns.logic:
1. Name the reporter (subject outside the quotes) — first-person words take its shape.
2. Name the listener (object of said to/told) — second-person words take its shape.
3. Third-person words copy straight across; check gender and number before finalising.

*Why it works:* every pronoun in the quote has exactly one anchor — reporter or listener — so the mapping is mechanical, not a matter of taste.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *He said to me, 'I will explain the sum to you.'*
example.solution: **He told me that he would explain the sum to me.** — I anchors to the reporter (he); you anchors to the listener (me). 'To you' forgets the listener; 'that I would explain' swaps the speaker.

patterns.name: tomorrow / next → the next / the following
patterns.howToSpot: The quote says tomorrow, next week, next Monday; options keep the word as it is or convert it to the next/the following.
patterns.logic:
1. Scan the quote for forward-pointing time words: tomorrow, next + unit.
2. Convert: tomorrow → the next day (or the following day); next Monday → the following Monday.
3. Confirm the verb shifted too (will → would) — the pair must move together.

*Why it works:* forward words are anchored to the day of speaking; once reported later, the anchor moves, so the word must move with it.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *Mother said, 'I will prepare your favourite dish tomorrow.'*
example.solution: **Mother said that she would prepare my favourite dish the next day.** — will → would AND tomorrow → the next day; your → my (the listener is the reporter).

patterns.name: yesterday / ago / last → the previous / before
patterns.howToSpot: The quote says yesterday, ago, last night/week; options keep ago/last or use the previous/the day before/the night before.
patterns.logic:
1. Scan for backward-pointing words: yesterday, ago, last + unit.
2. Convert: yesterday → the previous day; two years ago → two years before; last Sunday → the previous Sunday.
3. Check the verb took its step (V2 → had + V3) — ago and ago-keeping options are the planted faults.

*Why it works:* backward words measure from the day of speaking; from the reporter's later vantage point the same gap reads as 'before'.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The old man said, 'I bought this house forty years ago.'*
example.solution: **The old man said that he had bought that house forty years before.** — bought → had bought; ago → before; this → that. Keeping 'forty years ago' is the planted half-shift.

patterns.name: here / this / come → there / that / go
patterns.howToSpot: The quote contains place words or demonstratives (here, this, these, come, bring); options differ in whether they shifted.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline this/these/here/come/bring in the quote.
2. Shift: this → that, these → those, here → there, come → go, bring → take (viewpoint moves to the reporter's place).
3. Watch the double-that trap: said **that that** mango tree — the conjunction that followed by the demonstrative that is correct English.

*Why it works:* the reporter speaks from a different place than the original speaker, so near-pointing words must become far-pointing ones.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *Grandmother said, 'This mango tree was planted by my grandfather.'*
example.solution: **Grandmother said that that mango tree had been planted by her grandfather.** — this → that; my → her; was planted → had been planted. The double 'that that' is correct, not a typo.

subtopics.title: Questions, commands and exclamations
subtopics.concept:
Each sentence type has its own conversion skeleton:

**Yes/No questions:** asked + if/whether + statement order + backshift.
He said to me, "**Do you** know the answer?" → He asked me **if I knew** the answer. (The dummy 'do' vanishes; subject-auxiliary order flattens.)

**Wh-questions:** asked + wh-word + statement order + backshift.
She said to him, "**Where are you going**?" → She asked him **where he was going**.
He said to me, "**What did you eat**?" → He asked me **what I had eaten**.

**Commands/orders:** told/ordered + object + **to + V1** (negative: **not to** + V1).
The officer said to them, "Report immediately." → The officer ordered them **to report** immediately.
Mother said, "Don't touch the wire." → Mother told me **not to touch** the wire (or: **forbade me to touch**).

**Requests:** requested + object + to + V1. **Advice:** advised + object + to + V1.

**Let us (suggestion):** suggested + V-ing → He said, "Let us go for a walk" → He **suggested going** for a walk (or: suggested that they should go). **Let me (permission/allow):** requested to be allowed to → He said, "Let me sit here" → He requested that he might be allowed to sit there.

**Exclamations:** what/hurrah/alas/bravo carry the tone:
"Hurrah! We have won" → They **exclaimed with joy** that they had won.
"Alas! He is ruined" → He **exclaimed with sorrow** that he was ruined.
"Bravo! Well done" → They **applauded him, saying** that he had done well.
"Good morning" → wished; "Thank you" → thanked.

**Optatives (May God bless you):** prayed/wished — He said, "May you succeed!" → He **wished** that I might succeed.

tricks.title: Skeleton-first
tricks.body: Classify the quote (question/command/request/exclamation) and write its skeleton (asked if… / told … to … / exclaimed with joy that …). Then pour tense, pronoun and time-word shifts into the skeleton.

tricks.title: Do-support removal
tricks.body: Do/did in direct questions is a dummy — it disappears in indirect speech: 'Do you know' → if I knew, never 'if I did know'.

tricks.title: Exclamation-verb map
tricks.body: Hurrah → exclaimed with joy; Alas → exclaimed with sorrow; Bravo → applauded; Good morning → wished; Thank you → thanked. One-to-one map, no thinking needed.

mistakes: Keeping question order in reported questions ('asked where was I going').
Using 'if' with a wh-question.
Writing 'He ordered that I go' where the pattern is object + to + V1.
Using 'exclaimed with joy' for an Alas! sentence — tone verb mismatch.
subtopics.notes:
### Four skeletons, four connectors
- **Yes/No question**: asked + **if/whether** + statement order. 'Do you like filter coffee?' → He asked me **if I liked** filter coffee. The do/does/did of the quote dies and its tense lands on the main verb.
- **Wh-question**: asked + **the wh-word itself** + statement order. 'Where are you going?' → She asked me **where I was going**. The wh-word replaces if/whether — never both.
- **Command**: told / ordered + object + **to + V1**. 'Shut the door.' → He told me **to shut** the door. Negative: **not to** + V1. 'Do not shout.' → told him **not to shout**.
- **Request** (please, kindly): requested + object + to + V1. **Advice**: advised + object + to + V1. **Suggestion** (let us): suggested + V-ing, or proposed that they should go.

### Exclamations: read the emotion word first
| Direct marker | Reported frame |
|---|---|
| Hurrah! | exclaimed with joy that |
| Alas! | exclaimed with sorrow that |
| Bravo! | applauded him/her, saying that |
| What a / How + adjective | exclaimed that it was **very** + adjective |
| Good morning / Good night | wished (good night) |
| May you... (blessing/prayer) | prayed / wished that |

'What a beautiful view!' → He **exclaimed that it was a very** beautiful view. The exclamation mark becomes a full stop; the intensity moves into the word very.

### The statement-order test kills half the wrong options
After the connector, English is statement order: asked where he **had gone**, never *where had he gone*; asked if she **was coming**, never *if was she coming*. Combine it with the connector test — asked **that if** he was coming stacks two subordinators and dies on sight. These two faults together account for most planted wrong options in question items.

### Punctuation dies quietly
The question mark and the exclamation mark both become a full stop; the quotes and the comma vanish. An option that ends a reported question with a question mark is wrong even when every word in it is perfect — sweep the last character before the final option check.

### Verb choices that signal the type
asked (questions), ordered/told (commands), requested (please), advised (advice), suggested (let us), exclaimed (exclamations), wished/prayed (greetings, blessings). If the stem is a please-sentence and the option keys *ordered*, the item is over regardless of the tenses.

### Quick revision
- Yes/No → asked + if/whether + statement order; Wh → asked + wh + statement order; never that, never both, no do/does/did.
- Command → told/ordered + object + to + V1; negative → not to + V1; request → requested; advice → advised; let us → suggested + V-ing.
- Hurrah → exclaimed with joy; Alas → exclaimed with sorrow; What a → exclaimed that it was very.
- Reported questions and exclamations end in a full stop.
- Statement order after the connector — sweep every option for inverted auxiliaries first.

patterns.name: Yes/No question → asked + if/whether
patterns.howToSpot: The quote is answerable by yes or no (Do you...? Is there...? Can you...?); options differ in if/that and in the order after the connector.
patterns.logic:
1. Detect the yes/no shape (an auxiliary or do leads the quote).
2. Frame: asked + listener + if/whether + statement order, with do/does/did removed and the tense landed on the main verb.
3. Reject that-connectors, inverted orders (if was he), and retained do-forms.

*Why it works:* if/whether is the only subordinator that reports a closed question; everything else either mislabels the question or breaks the order.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *My aunt said to me, 'Do you like filter coffee?'*
example.solution: **My aunt asked me if I liked filter coffee.** — do dies, liked carries the past; you → I (listener = reporter). 'If did I like' keeps the do and inverts the order.

patterns.name: Wh-question → asked + wh + statement order
patterns.howToSpot: The quote opens with why/where/when/what/who/how; the wrong options invert the auxiliary (why did I) or stack that before the wh-word.
patterns.logic:
1. Copy the wh-word as the connector — nothing before it (no that).
2. Restore statement order: wh + subject + verb, backshifted one rung.
3. Delete do/does/did; the past lands on the main verb (do you want → I wanted).

*Why it works:* a reported wh-question is a noun clause in statement shape; keeping the question order is the single most planted fault in the section.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The interviewer asked me, 'Why do you want this job?'*
example.solution: **The interviewer asked me why I wanted that job.** — do dies (want → wanted); you → I; this → that. 'Why did I want' keeps both the do and the inversion.

patterns.name: Command → told/ordered + object + to + V1
patterns.howToSpot: The quote is a bare order, often negative (Do not...); options differ in to/not to placement, or keep the imperative verb bare.
patterns.logic:
1. Positive order: ordered/told + object + to + V1.
2. Negative order: not goes BEFORE to — not to make a noise.
3. this/these in the order shift to that/those; the tone verb must match (order, not request).

*Why it works:* the infinitive is the only frame that reports an order; the negative particle always sits outside the to, never inside the verb phrase.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The teacher said to the boys, 'Do not make a noise in the library.'*
example.solution: **The teacher ordered the boys not to make a noise in the library.** — the negative rides before to; make stays a base verb. 'Not making' breaks the frame; dropping not reverses the order.

patterns.name: Request and advice frames
patterns.howToSpot: The quote carries please/kindly (request) or advice sense (Give up..., Always speak...); the options verb between requested/advised/ordered.
patterns.logic:
1. please/kindly → requested + object + to + V1.
2. Advice → advised + object + to + V1 (always/never ride before the verb: advised him always to speak...).
3. The listener is compulsory and in the object case: requested the doctor, never requested to the doctor.

*Why it works:* requests and advice share the to-infinitive frame with orders; only the reporting verb separates them, so the verb is where the item is decided.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The patient said to the doctor, 'Please prescribe a milder tablet.'*
example.solution: **The patient requested the doctor to prescribe a milder tablet.** — please → requested; the doctor is the object of requested, not of a stray to. 'Ordered the doctor' hardens a plea into a command.

patterns.name: Exclamation → exclaimed with joy/sorrow that
patterns.howToSpot: The quote carries Hurrah/Alas/What a/How; options differ in joy/sorrow, in exclaimed vs said, and in the very-conversion of What a.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the emotion word: Hurrah → with joy; Alas → with sorrow; Bravo → applauded...saying.
2. Frame: exclaimed with joy/sorrow + that + statement (backshifted).
3. What a/How + adjective → it was very + adjective; the exclamation mark becomes a full stop.

*Why it works:* the reported frame must carry the same emotion as the quote; joy and sorrow are the classic planted swap.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The players said, 'Hurrah! We have clinched the series.'*
example.solution: **The players exclaimed with joy that they had clinched the series.** — joy for Hurrah; have clinched → had clinched. 'With sorrow' reverses the emotion; 'said with joy' loses the exclamation frame.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy: the four-check protocol
subtopics.concept:
Every narration item changes the quote in exactly four dimensions. Check them in order — each wrong option in the paper fails exactly one:

1. **Reporting verb + connective.** Tone-fit verb (asked/told/ordered/requested/exclaimed); that / if / wh-word connective. Kills options with 'said me', 'asked that' (for yes/no), missing if.
2. **Tense.** Backshift by the ladder — unless the quote is a universal truth or the reporting verb is present. Kills options with unchanged or over-shifted tenses.
3. **Pronouns.** SONA sweep: speaker, listener, unchanged third. Kills options where I/me/you/he are tangled.
4. **Time/place words.** yesterday → the previous day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that, now → then. Kills options that leave 'today' stranded in reported speech.

**Both directions appear:** direct→indirect dominates (3 of 4 items), but indirect→direct appears in every 4th shift or so — run the same four checks backwards (restore quotes, comma and question order, un-backshift past perfect to past simple, restore today/yesterday).

**Daily plan:** 10 conversions a day alternating statement/question/command types, written by hand. In a week the four checks run in parallel; in two, narration is a free mark. Tier 1 carries two narration items; Tier 2 carries more, often inside error-spotting.

tricks.title: One-fault elimination
tricks.body: Name the fault of each wrong option — verb, tense, pronoun or time-word. If you can't name a fault, look again; if two options share none, you've misjudged the tone verb.

tricks.title: Reverse-mode anchors
tricks.body: Indirect→direct: the phrase 'the previous day' signals quotes needed with 'yesterday'; 'asked if' signals a yes/no question with inverted order and dummy 'do' if present tense returns.

tricks.title: Written drill
tricks.body: Narration lives in punctuation and word order — practise on paper, never orally; the hand catches what the ear forgives.

mistakes: Running checks out of order and fixing tense while leaving 'said me' intact.
Un-backshifting 'had seen' to 'had seen' in direct speech (it must become saw).
Forgetting the comma and quotes in indirect→direct answers.
Assuming every tense shifts — the truth-sentence exception costs a mark when ignored.
subtopics.notes:
### The four-check protocol (run it in this order)
1. **Connector**: that / if-whether / the wh-word / to + V1 — must match the sentence type, and there must be exactly one.
2. **Reporting verb**: said to + listener → told/asked; the tone must match (requested vs ordered vs advised vs exclaimed vs suggested).
3. **Tense ladder**: one rung down for a past frame; past perfect stays; universal truths stay; would/could/might/should/used to freeze.
4. **Pronouns + time/place**: SONA mapping; the tomorrow→the next day family; this→that, here→there.

Work in this order because connector faults are the cheapest to see — you can kill two options in five seconds without reading a verb. In a well-set item every wrong option breaks exactly one check, so name the check that killed it.

### Reverse conversion (indirect → direct)
1. Put the reporting verb back with its comma and quotes: told me → said to me, '...'
2. Remove the connector: that disappears; if/whether becomes an auxiliary-led question (Are you...?); the wh-word stays but question order returns.
3. Step the tense back UP one rung: had + V3 → V2; was + V-ing → is/am + V-ing; would → will; could → can; had to → must.
4. Reverse the pronouns (SONA backwards): told me he → 'I'; told her that she → 'you'.
5. Restore the final punctuation: ? for questions, ! for exclamations.

*Told the students that the earth revolves around the sun* → **said to the students, 'The earth revolves around the sun.'** Note the universal truth did not need un-shifting — that is exactly why the exam picks it.

### Planted faults, ranked by how often they appear
1. Statement order broken: *asked if was he coming*.
2. Half-backshift: *said that he is busy*.
3. Tense shifted but the time word left behind: *would visit tomorrow*.
4. told with no object, or requested **to** the doctor.
5. Connector stacking: *asked that why*, *told that to come*.
6. Stray punctuation: a reported question still ending in a question mark.
7. Wrong tone verb: please keyed as ordered; Hurrah keyed as sorrow.

### The 25-second routine
Read the direct sentence and name its TYPE before touching the options — statement, yes/no, wh, command, request, exclamation. Pre-write the skeleton in your head: *asked if + was...* or *ordered + object + not to...*. Then match options against the skeleton, one check at a time, first match to all four checks wins. Ten items a day for a week makes the ladder automatic; after that the section is free marks.

### Quick revision
- Four checks in order: connector → reporting verb → tense ladder → pronouns/time.
- Reverse: quotes and comma back, connector out, tense up one rung, pronouns back, punctuation restored.
- Top faults: inverted order after the connector, half-backshift, time word left behind, object-less told, double connector, stray question mark.
- Name the sentence TYPE first; pre-write the skeleton; then read the options.
- Every wrong option breaks exactly one check — name it and move on.

patterns.name: Four-check elimination on a full item
patterns.howToSpot: A straightforward statement item where each wrong option fails a different check — one keeps said to, one skips the backshift, one keeps yesterday.
patterns.logic:
1. Connector first: told + listener + that is mandatory for a statement with a named listener.
2. Tense ladder: every verb steps one rung (was → had been).
3. Time words: yesterday → the previous day.
4. Pronouns: SONA (I → he, my → his/her).

*Why it works:* running the checks in a fixed order turns a four-way comparison into four yes/no questions, each settled in a glance.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The manager said to the clerk, 'You were absent yesterday.'*
example.solution: **The manager told the clerk that he had been absent the previous day.** — told (not said to); were → had been; yesterday → the previous day; you → he. Each wrong option drops exactly one of these.

patterns.name: Reverse conversion (indirect to direct)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem is already reported and the options are direct quotes; they differ in quotes/comma, in the un-shift, and in question order.
patterns.logic:
1. Rebuild the frame: said to + listener, comma, quotes.
2. Drop the connector; for reported questions, restore auxiliary-first order and the question mark.
3. Step the tense up one rung (had + V3 → V2; would → will); frozen forms (revolves for a truth) stay.
4. Reverse the pronouns before closing the quote.

*Why it works:* the direct form must reproduce what the speaker plausibly said — every reported-layer word (that, had, would) has to dissolve back.

example.q: Select the direct form: *The teacher told the students that the earth revolves around the sun.*
example.solution: **The teacher said to the students, 'The earth revolves around the sun.'** — quotes return, that vanishes, and the universal truth keeps its present. 'That the earth...' left inside quotes is the planted fault.

patterns.name: Connector-stacking and modal-question faults
patterns.howToSpot: Polite questions (Shall I...?, Could you...?) reported with that if, or with the modal kept as will/can.
patterns.logic:
1. Shall I...? (seeking instruction) → asked + if + should/might + V1; Could you...? → asked + if + could + V1.
2. Exactly one connector; now/then-type shifts ride along (now → then).
3. The modal must step down (will → would, can → could), never stay put and never leap to must.

*Why it works:* polite-question items stack three checks at once — connector, modal, time word — so each option fails a different one.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The clerk said to the manager, 'Shall I close the register now?'*
example.solution: **The clerk asked the manager if he should close the register then.** — Shall I → if he should; now → then. 'That if' stacks connectors; 'if he will close' skips the modal shift.

patterns.name: Statement-order and punctuation sweep
patterns.howToSpot: Wh-question items where two options share every word but one inverts the auxiliary (when would the rains vs when the rains would) or keeps a final question mark.
patterns.logic:
1. After the wh-word, demand subject + verb: asked when the rains WOULD come.
2. Kill inverted orders (when would the rains come) instantly.
3. Sweep the final character: a reported question ends in a full stop, never a question mark.

*Why it works:* order and punctuation faults are invisible when reading for meaning, so they must be checked mechanically, word-position by word-position.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The child asked her mother, 'When will the rains come?'*
example.solution: **The child asked her mother when the rains would come.** — will steps to would and moves AFTER the subject; the question mark becomes a full stop. Both faults sit in the decoys.

patterns.name: Modal + time-word double check
patterns.howToSpot: Items where the quote carries a modal (may, could have) AND a time word (next week, yesterday); wrong options fix one and forget the other.
patterns.logic:
1. Handle the modal first: may → might; could have stays could have (frozen).
2. Handle the time word second: next week → the following week; yesterday → the previous day.
3. Verify BOTH moved — the partial-shift option is the planted trap.

*Why it works:* setters split the shift across two dimensions; candidates who check only the tense fall for the untouched time word.

example.q: Select the indirect form: *The coach said, 'The trials may be postponed till next week.'*
example.solution: **The coach said that the trials might be postponed till the following week.** — may → might AND next week → the following week. Either shift alone is the planted half-answer.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A declarative quote after said/said to; the options are that-clauses differing in the tense rung (was vs had been), in the time word (today vs that day), or in said-to vs told.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert the frame first: said to + listener becomes told + listener, add that. Then step every verb one rung down the ladder (am → was, wrote → had written, will → would), map pronouns by SONA, and shift the time words (today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, ago → before). Universal truths keep their tense.

example.q: Select the indirect form: 'He said, "I bought a car yesterday."'
example.solution: *He said that he **had bought** a car **the previous day*** — bought steps to had bought and yesterday to the previous day; I follows the reporter (he).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The quote ends with a question mark; the options differ in the connector (if/whether vs that vs the wh-word), in statement vs question order, and in whether do/does/did survived.
pyqPatterns.approach: Yes/No question → asked + if/whether + statement order. Wh-question → asked + the wh-word alone + statement order. Kill do/does/did and land the tense on the main verb (Do you like → if I liked). The final mark is a full stop, never a question mark.

example.q: Select the indirect form: 'The stranger said to me, "Can you show me the way to the station?"'
example.solution: *The stranger asked me **if I could show him** the way to the station* — one connector, statement order, can → could, you/me remapped by SONA.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The quote is an order (bare verb), a please-sentence, advice, or carries Hurrah/Alas/What a; the options differ in the reporting verb (ordered/requested/advised/exclaimed) and in the to/not-to frame.
pyqPatterns.approach: Order → told/ordered + object + to + V1 (negative: not to V1). Request → requested + object + to + V1. Advice → advised + object + to + V1. Exclamation → match the emotion: Hurrah → exclaimed with joy that; Alas → exclaimed with sorrow that; What a + adj → exclaimed that it was very + adj. The tone verb decides the item before any tense does.

example.q: Select the indirect form: 'Mother said to me, "Do not go out in the rain."'
example.solution: *Mother told me **not to go** out in the rain* — a negative order rides not before to; the mother's concern keeps the neutral told frame.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem is already reported (told/asked + that/if/wh) and the options are quoted sentences differing in the quotes-and-comma frame, in the un-shift, and in question order.
pyqPatterns.approach: Rebuild the frame (said to + listener, comma, quotes), drop the connector, step the tense UP one rung (had + V3 → V2, would → will, had to → must), reverse the pronouns (told me he → 'I'), and restore question order and the ? for questions. Universal truths need no un-shift.

example.q: Select the direct form: 'He asked me if I was hungry.'
example.solution: *He said to me, **'Are you hungry?'*** — if dissolves into an auxiliary-led question, was steps back to are, I returns to you, and the question mark returns.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Reporting verb choice: say vs tell and tone verbs
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options that keep said to, drop the listener after told, or swap the tone verb (requested vs ordered vs advised) while the tenses are identical.
pyqPatterns.approach: said to + person → told + person (tell never takes to, say never takes a listener). Then match the tone: please → requested; command → ordered; advice → advised; suggestion → suggested; Hurrah/Alas → exclaimed with joy/sorrow. A present frame (says/has said) freezes the quote's tense.

example.q: Select the indirect form: 'She said to me, "I am very busy today."'
example.solution: *She **told me** that she was very busy that day* — said to me must become told me; keeping 'said to me that...' is the planted fault, as is an objectless 'told that...'

pyqPatterns.pattern: Backshift ladder and the no-shift exceptions
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options differing only in the verb phrase (was learning / had been learning / is learning) or a universal truth offered with rose instead of rises.
pyqPatterns.approach: One rung down for a past frame: present → past, past → past perfect, past continuous → past perfect continuous, will/can/may → would/could/might, must (duty) → had to. Refuse both neighbours: the untouched present (half-backshift) and the double-step past perfect (over-backshift). Exceptions: universal truths, present reporting verbs, and frozen forms (would rather, used to, could have) do not move.

example.q: Select the indirect form: 'The teacher said, "The earth revolves around the sun."'
example.solution: *The teacher said that the earth **revolves** around the sun* — a universal truth keeps the present even inside said; 'revolved' is the classic planted backshift.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Pronoun and time-word mapping (SONA + the time table)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options differing only in pronouns (to me / to you / to him) or in the time word (tomorrow vs the next day; ago vs before) — often paired with a shifted or unshifted verb.
pyqPatterns.approach: SONA: first person follows the reporter, second person follows the listener, third person never changes — and track gender before his/her. Time table: tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, ago → before, now → then, today → that day, next → the following, last → the previous; this → that, here → there, come → go. Tense and time words must move together — a half-shift is always the planted option.

example.q: Select the indirect form: 'He said, "The minister will visit our town tomorrow."'
example.solution: *He said that the minister **would** visit our town **the next day*** — will and tomorrow move as a pair; shifting only one is the standard decoy.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "I am writing a letter."
options: He said that he has written a letter.
He said that him was writing a letter.
He said that he was writing a letter.
He said that he is writing a letter.
solvedExamples.solution: Reporting verb 'said' is past → backshift present continuous to **past continuous** (was writing), and the pronoun I → **he** (speaker). B skips the backshift; C jumps two steps; D uses the object-case 'him' as subject.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Past reporter → one step back: am writing → was writing; I → he.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said to him, "Where are you going?"
options: She asked him where was he going.
She asked him that where he was going.
She asked him where he is going.
She asked him where he was going.
solvedExamples.solution: Wh-question → keep the wh-word, flatten to **statement order** (where he was — not 'was he'), backshift (are → was), you → he. B keeps question order; C doubles the connective ('that' with a wh-word); D skips the backshift.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Wh-word + statement order + backshift. 'that' never accompanies a wh-word.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The teacher said to the students, "The earth revolves around the sun."
options: The teacher told to the students that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher told the students that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher told the students that the earth revolved around the sun.
The teacher said to the students that the earth had revolved around the sun.
solvedExamples.solution: A **universal truth keeps its tense** even after a past reporting verb — 'revolves' stays. said to + listener → **told** + listener. B wrongly backshifts; C over-shifts to past perfect; D writes 'told to'.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Truth test: facts of nature freeze — revolves, not revolved.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said to me, "I will meet you tomorrow."
options: She told me that she will meet me the next day.
She told me that she would meet you the next day.
She said me that she would meet me the next day.
She told me that she would meet me the next day.
practice.solution: said to me → told me; will → **would**; you → **me** (listener); tomorrow → **the next day**. B skips the backshift; C leaves 'you' unconverted; D writes the impossible 'said me'.
practice.shortcut: Four checks: told + would + me + next day.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "I bought a car yesterday."
options: He said that he had bought a car the previous day.
He said that he bought a car the previous day.
He said that he has bought a car yesterday.
He said that he had bought a car yesterday.
practice.solution: Simple past → **past perfect** (had bought); yesterday → **the previous day**. B stops at simple past; C keeps 'yesterday'; D shifts tense but strands 'yesterday' — both dimensions must move.
practice.shortcut: Past → past perfect, and yesterday travels to 'the previous day'.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Mother said to me, "Do not go out in the rain."
options: Mother said me not to go out in the rain.
Mother told me to not going out in the rain.
Mother told me don't go out in the rain.
Mother told me not to go out in the rain.
practice.solution: Negative command → **told + object + not to + V1**. B uses 'said me'; C breaks the to-structure; D keeps the direct form 'don't'.
practice.shortcut: Negative order skeleton: told + me + not to + go.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The stranger said to me, "Can you show me the way to the station?"
options: The stranger asked me that I could show him the way to the station.
The stranger asked me if I can show him the way to the station.
The stranger asked me if I could show me the way to the station.
The stranger asked me if I could show him the way to the station.
practice.solution: Yes/no question → **asked + if** + statement order + backshift (can → could); you → I (listener), me → him (speaker). B uses 'that' with a yes/no question; C skips the backshift; D tangles the two pronouns.
practice.shortcut: if/whether for yes/no; can → could; pronouns swap by SONA.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

They said, "Hurrah! We have won the trophy."
options: They said with joy that they have won the trophy.
They exclaimed with joy that they would win the trophy.
They exclaimed with joy that they had won the trophy.
They exclaimed with sorrow that they had won the trophy.
practice.solution: Hurrah → **exclaimed with joy**; present perfect → past perfect; we → they. B inverts the tone; C keeps the un-shifted 'have won'; D changes the tense to would.
practice.shortcut: Hurrah = joy, Alas = sorrow; then backshift the tense.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

He asked me if I was hungry.
options: He said to me, "Are you hungry?"
He said to me, "You are hungry."
He said to me, "Was I hungry?"
He said to me, "Are I hungry?"
practice.solution: 'asked if' = yes/no question → restore quotes, question order and **present tense** (was → are), you as listener. B states instead of asking; C reverses the pronouns; D writes the impossible 'Are I'.
practice.shortcut: Reverse: if + was → Are you …? with question mark.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said, "I have finished my work."
options: She said that she has finished her work.
She said that she finished her work.
She said that she had finish her work.
She said that she had finished her work.
practice.solution: Present perfect → **past perfect**: had finished; I → she; my → her. B skips the backshift; C drops to simple past; D breaks the participle.
practice.shortcut: have finished → had finished.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said to me, "Please lend me your pen."
options: He requested me to lend him my pen.
He requested me to lend me your pen.
He ordered me to lend him my pen.
He said to me please to lend him my pen.
practice.solution: Please → **requested**; to lend + him (speaker) + my (listener). B leaves both pronouns direct; C mismatches tone (ordered for a request); D has no sentence structure.
practice.shortcut: please sets the verb: requested; then him + my.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

They said, "We shall visit Agra next month."
options: They said that they will visit Agra the following month.
They said that they would visit Agra next month.
They said that they should visit Agra the following month.
They said that they would visit Agra the following month.
practice.solution: shall → **would** (with we/they in the past frame); next month → **the following month**. B skips the modal backshift; C strands 'next month'; D swaps shall for should, changing meaning.
practice.shortcut: shall → would; next → the following.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The doctor said to the patient, "Give up smoking."
options: The doctor advised the patient giving up smoking.
The doctor said to the patient to giving up smoking.
The doctor advised the patient to give up smoking.
The doctor advised to the patient to give up smoking.
practice.solution: Advice command → **advised + object + to + V1**. B adds a stray 'to' after advised; C drops the infinitive; D both breaks structure and keeps 'said to' where the tone verb fits.
practice.shortcut: advice skeleton: advised + object + to + give.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "Alas! I am ruined."
options: He said with sorrow that he is ruined.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he is ruined.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he was ruined.
He exclaimed with joy that he was ruined.
practice.solution: Alas → **exclaimed with sorrow**; am → was (backshift); I → he. B inverts the tone; C leaves the tense; D strands 'is'.
practice.shortcut: Alas = sorrow; am → was.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

She said that she had seen him the day before.
options: She said, "I saw him yesterday."
She said, "I had seen him yesterday."
She said, "I have seen him yesterday."
She said, "I saw him the previous day."
practice.solution: 'the day before' → **yesterday**; past perfect → **simple past** (saw) when the time anchor is restored; she → I, him stays. B keeps 'had seen' inside quotes; C pairs present perfect with yesterday (impossible); D leaves reported time words in a quote.
practice.shortcut: Reverse ladder: had + V3 → V2 when the anchor returns as yesterday.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said to her, "What did you eat for breakfast?"
options: He asked her what she had eaten for breakfast.
He asked her what she ate for breakfast.
He asked her what did she eat for breakfast.
He asked her what she has eaten for breakfast.
practice.solution: Wh-question: keep 'what', flatten order, **past simple → past perfect** (did … eat → had eaten), you → she. B under-shifts; C keeps question order with dummy 'did'; D mis-shifts to present perfect.
practice.shortcut: did + eat → had eaten; statement order after 'what'.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Ram said to Shyam, "You must bring your book tomorrow."
options: Ram told Shyam that he musted bring his book the next day.
Ram told Shyam that he had to bring his book tomorrow.
Ram told Shyam that you had to bring his book the next day.
Ram told Shyam that he had to bring his book the next day.
practice.solution: must → **had to**; you → **he** (the listener Shyam); your → his; tomorrow → **the next day**. B invents 'musted'; C strands 'tomorrow'; D leaves 'you' in place.
practice.shortcut: must → had to; listener's pronouns follow Shyam.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The boys said, "Let us play football."
options: The boys told that they played football.
The boys asked if they played football.
The boys suggested playing football.
The boys suggested to play football.
practice.solution: 'Let us' = suggestion → **suggested + V-ing** (or suggested that they should play). B breaks the gerund pattern; C misreads it as a statement; D misreads it as a question.
practice.shortcut: Let us → suggested + V-ing.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said to me, "I am very busy today."
options: She told me that she was very busy that day.
She said to me that she was very busy that day.
She told me that she is very busy today.
She told me that she had been very busy that day.
practice.solution: said to me becomes **told me**; am steps to **was**; today becomes **that day**; I follows the reporter (she). Keeping 'said to me' refuses the verb change; 'is very busy today' skips both shifts; 'had been' climbs two rungs.
practice.shortcut: said to + person = told + person. Then ladder and time words.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The manager said to the staff, "We have finalised the schedule."
options: The manager said to the staff that they had finalised the schedule.
The manager told the staff that they have finalised the schedule.
The manager told the staff that they had finalised the schedule.
The manager told to the staff that they had finalised the schedule.
practice.solution: **told the staff** — said to vanishes, told takes its listener directly (never 'told to'); have steps to **had**; we follows the reporters (they). 'Said to the staff' keeps the direct frame; 'have finalised' skips the rung.
practice.shortcut: told + listener, no 'to'. have/has → had.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

My neighbour said to me, "Your gate is squeaking again."
options: My neighbour said to me that my gate was squeaking again.
My neighbour told me that your gate is squeaking again.
My neighbour told that my gate was squeaking again.
My neighbour told me that my gate was squeaking again.
practice.solution: said to me → **told me**; your anchors to the listener, so it becomes **my**; is steps to **was**. 'Your gate is squeaking' leaves both the pronoun and the tense unshifted; 'told that...' drops the listener that told demands.
practice.shortcut: told needs its listener; you → me when I am the listener.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The doctor said to Father, "Give up smoking."
options: The doctor requested Father to give up smoking.
The doctor advised Father giving up smoking.
The doctor advised that Father gives up smoking.
The doctor advised Father to give up smoking.
practice.solution: The quote is advice, so the frame is **advised + object + to + V1**: *advised Father to give up smoking.* 'Requested Father' turns advice into a plea; 'advised Father giving' breaks the infinitive frame; a that-clause after advised is the wrong connector for this tone.
practice.shortcut: Advice → advised + object + to + V1.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The guard said to us, "Please show your ID cards."
options: The guard ordered us to show our ID cards.
The guard requested us showing our ID cards.
The guard requested us to show our ID cards.
The guard requested to us that show our ID cards.
practice.solution: Please marks a request: **requested us to show our ID cards.** The listener sits directly after requested (never 'to us'); the verb after to stays in base form. 'Ordered us' hardens a polite plea into a command; 'requested us showing' swaps the infinitive for a gerund.
practice.shortcut: please → requested + object + to + V1.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The captain said to the players, "Report for practice at six sharp."
options: The captain requested the players to report for practice at six sharp.
The captain ordered the players reporting for practice at six sharp.
The captain ordered the players to report for practice at six sharp.
The captain ordered that the players report for practice at six sharp.
practice.solution: A drill instruction is an order: **ordered the players to report for practice at six sharp.** 'Requested the players' softens a command wrongly; 'ordered the players reporting' breaks the to-frame; the that-clause belongs to statements, not orders.
practice.shortcut: No please + a task = ordered + object + to + V1.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Ravi says, "I do not like loud music."
options: Ravi says that he did not like loud music.
Ravi said that he does not like loud music.
Ravi says that he is not liking loud music.
Ravi says that he does not like loud music.
practice.solution: The frame **says** is in the present, so NO backshift: the quote keeps **does not like**. Only the pronoun moves (I → he). 'Did not like' backshifts without cause; swapping says to said changes the reporting verb itself; 'is not liking' garbles the simple present.
practice.shortcut: says/asks = present frame = tense frozen.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Mother often says, "Honesty is the best policy."
options: Mother often says that honesty was the best policy.
Mother often said that honesty is the best policy.
Mother often says that honesty is the better policy.
Mother often says that honesty is the best policy.
practice.solution: Present frame **says** keeps the quote in the present: **is the best policy** — doubly safe because the sentence is also a universal truth. 'Was the best policy' backshifts twice wrongly; 'often said' moves the reporting verb; 'the better policy' corrupts the superlative.
practice.shortcut: Present frame + universal truth = nothing shifts.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The teacher has said, "The exam will begin at ten."
options: The teacher has said that the exam would begin at ten.
The teacher has said that the exam will begin at ten.
The teacher said that the exam will begin at ten.
The teacher has said that the exam will be begun at ten.
practice.solution: The present perfect frame **has said** is still a present reporting verb — no backshift: **will begin** stays. 'Would begin' applies a past-frame rule to a present frame; 'The teacher said' downgrades the frame; 'will be begun' pushes a future simple into a passive.
practice.shortcut: has said is present too — the ladder is not climbed.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Priya asked me, "Are you coming to the fair?"
options: Priya asked me that was I coming to the fair.
Priya asked me if I was coming to the fair.
Priya asked me if was I coming to the fair.
Priya asked me that if I was coming to the fair.
practice.solution: A yes/no question reports with ONE connector: **asked me if I was coming to the fair.** — if + statement order, are stepping to was. 'That was I' uses a statement connector for a question; 'if was I coming' inverts the order; 'that if' stacks two subordinators.
practice.shortcut: Yes/no → asked + if + statement order. One connector.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The officer said to her, "Why have you not submitted the form?"
options: The officer asked her that why she had not submitted the form.
The officer asked her why had she not submitted the form.
The officer asked her why she had not submitted the form.
The officer asked her that she had not submitted the form.
practice.solution: The wh-word itself is the connector: **asked her why she had not submitted the form.** Nothing may precede it. 'That why' stacks connectors; 'why had she' keeps question order; dropping why turns the question into a false statement.
practice.shortcut: wh-word stands alone — no that, no inversion.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The coach said to the team, "Never give up in the final minutes."
options: The coach advised the team not give up in the final minutes.
The coach advised to the team never to give up in the final minutes.
The coach advised the team never to give up in the final minutes.
The coach ordered the team never to giving up in the final minutes.
practice.solution: Encouragement in imperative form is advice: **advised the team never to give up in the final minutes.** — never rides before to. 'Not give up' loses both the to and the never; 'advised to the team' inserts a to that advised never takes; 'never to giving up' swaps the base verb for a gerund.
practice.shortcut: never/always sit before to: advised him never to repeat it.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "I am learning German these days."
options: He said that he is learning German those days.
He said that he had been learning German those days.
He said that he learns German those days.
He said that he was learning German those days.
practice.solution: Present continuous steps one rung: **was learning** — not the untouched 'is learning' and not the double-step 'had been learning'. I follows the reporter (he); these days becomes **those days**.
practice.shortcut: am/is + V-ing → was/were + V-ing. One rung only.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said, "I write short stories."
options: She said that she writes short stories.
She said that she had written short stories.
She said that she wrote short stories.
She said that she was writing short stories.
practice.solution: Simple present steps to simple past: **wrote**. 'Writes' skips the ladder; 'had written' overshoots by a full rung; 'was writing' changes the aspect from habit to an ongoing act.
practice.shortcut: V1 → V2 inside said. Habit stays a habit.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

They said, "We watched the eclipse together."
options: They said that they watched the eclipse together.
They said that they have watched the eclipse together.
They said that they had watched the eclipse together.
They said that they were watching the eclipse together.
practice.solution: Simple past steps to past perfect: **had watched** — the eclipse-watching happened before the saying. 'Watched' keeps both events at the same level; 'have watched' imports a present perfect the past frame cannot host; 'were watching' changes the aspect.
practice.shortcut: V2 → had + V3. The earlier event climbs.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The watchman said, "The lights were flickering all night."
options: The watchman said that the lights were flickering all night.
The watchman said that the lights had flickered all night.
The watchman said that the lights have been flickering all night.
The watchman said that the lights had been flickering all night.
practice.solution: Past continuous steps to past perfect continuous: **had been flickering**. 'Were flickering' stays on the direct rung; 'had flickered' collapses the ongoing act into a completed one; 'have been flickering' drags a present form into a past frame.
practice.shortcut: was/were + V-ing → had been + V-ing.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said, "I can solve this puzzle."
options: She said that she can solve that puzzle.
She said that she may solve that puzzle.
She said that she could solve that puzzle.
She said that she will solve that puzzle.
practice.solution: can steps to **could**, and this → **that**: *she could solve that puzzle.* 'Can solve' refuses the shift; 'may solve' and 'will solve' import different modals entirely — each modal has exactly one partner one rung down.
practice.shortcut: can→could, may→might, will→would. Nothing else.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said, "The minister will visit our town tomorrow."
options: He said that the minister would visit our town the next day.
He said that the minister will visit our town the next day.
He said that the minister would visit our town tomorrow.
He said that the minister had visited our town the next day.
practice.solution: will steps to **would**, and tomorrow becomes **the next day** — the modal and the time word move together. Keeping either one while shifting the other is the planted half-shift; 'had visited' swaps the future for a past perfect.
practice.shortcut: will → would AND tomorrow → the next day. Both or neither.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The teacher said, "The sun rises in the east."
options: The teacher said that the sun rises in the east.
The teacher said that the sun rose in the east.
The teacher said that the sun had risen in the east.
The teacher said that the sun is rising in the east.
practice.solution: A universal truth does not backshift: **rises** stays in the present even inside said. 'Rose' applies the ladder to a law of nature; 'had risen' doubles the error; 'is rising' changes the statement from a permanent fact to a momentary scene.
practice.shortcut: Truths of nature keep their tense — however past the frame is.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

My grandfather often said, "Time is the best healer."
options: My grandfather often said that time was the best healer.
My grandfather often said that time is the best healer.
My grandfather often says that time is the best healer.
My grandfather often said that time would be the best healer.
practice.solution: A proverb is a universal truth — the tense stays: **time is the best healer**. 'Was the best' backshifts the proverb; 'often says' alters the reporting frame the stem gives; 'would be' inserts a future the quote never had.
practice.shortcut: Proverbs and laws: is stays is.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Ravi said, "I would rather stay at home."
options: Ravi said that he had rather stayed at home.
Ravi said that he will rather stay at home.
Ravi said that he would rather stay at home.
Ravi said that he would rather stayed at home.
practice.solution: would rather is a frozen preference form — it never shifts: **he would rather stay at home.** Only the pronoun moves (I → he). 'Had rather stayed' invents a rung the ladder does not have; 'will rather' swaps the modal; 'would rather stayed' breaks the base verb after rather.
practice.shortcut: would rather / had better / used to: copy them as they are.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said, "I used to swim every morning."
options: She said that she had used to swim every morning.
She said that she used to swim every morning.
She said that she used to swam every morning.
She said that she had been used to swim every morning.
practice.solution: used to is already a past-habit form and freezes in reported speech: **she used to swim every morning.** 'Had used to' adds an impossible rung; 'used to swam' corrupts the base verb after to; 'been used to' turns the habit phrase into a passive.
practice.shortcut: used to does not climb — only the pronoun moves.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said to me, "I will explain the sum to you."
options: He told me that he would explain the sum to me.
He told me that he would explain the sum to you.
